en: Every day,
a general cognition of substrata is indeed admitted; that [cognition] depends upon the causal complex consisting of the sense organ and the awareness of its properties.

The proximity of the loci occurs through the same relation by which the universal is known; however, in a case where, after the destruction of a particular jar, there arises a recollection of that which possessed that jar,
there would be no manifestation of all those things possessing that jar through the universal-characterized perception (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*).

Because at that time the universal does not exist. Furthermore, why would such a cognition— "it is a jar"— not arise on the following day, even without sensory contact, given that the universal which serves as the qualifier of that cognition exists there?

Therefore, he says that the cognition whose object is the universal is produced from that [perception], and thus it is the *pratyāsatti* (proximity), not the universal itself—this is what he means by "the *pratyāsatti*. Here, *pratyāsatti* means proximity (*āsatti*). Consequently, in the term *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*, the word *lakṣaṇa* has the sense of "object" (*viṣaya*); by this [he explains the compound].
The meaning obtained is that the cognition having a universal (sāmānya) as its object constitutes the "proximity" (pratyāsatti). Now, one might object:

if a cognition of a universal were to occur even without the contact of the eye and so forth, then there would be visual perception of all jars and other such things [simultaneously]; therefore, he says "that" (tat). This is the meaning of it.

When a cognition of a general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is to be produced by an external sense faculty, then, in relation to any given substratum (*dharmin*), there is required a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) for the cognition of that general characteristic produced by that sense faculty; and that causal complex consists of the contact of the eye, the contact of light, and so forth. Therefore, in darkness and similar conditions, [the cognition does not arise] through the eye and other such faculties.

Such a cognition is not produced. [Objection: Now, if the cognitive proximity characterized by cognition (*jñānalakṣaṇāpratyāsatti*) is of the nature of cognition, and the universal-characterized proximity (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*) is also of the nature of cognition, then there would be no distinction between the two; therefore, he says: "The object-possessor... For the proximity characterized by the universal has as its object the cognition of that which is its substratum.

But the proximity characterized by knowledge (*jñānalakṣaṇāpratyāsatti*) is the proximity only of that which is the object of the knowledge; this is the meaning here: in perception, manifestation without a sense-contact is not possible, and thus, without the generality-characterized proximity (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), all instances of smoke [could not be manifested] as "smoke-ness."
Furthermore, how could there be the manifestation of all fires through the manifestation of a single fire?

For that purpose, the universal-characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇā) is accepted. Nor should it be argued that there is no harm in the absence of the manifestation of all fires and all smokes; for the relation of fire with smoke has already been apprehended in the case of the perceptible smoke.

Furthermore, since no other smoke is present, the doubt as to whether "smoke is pervaded by fire" or "not" would be untenable; however, in my view, when all smoke is presented through *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* (the generalizing character),
with respect to smoke existing at another time and place...
A doubt regarding the non-pervasion of the probans by the probandum is possible.

Nor should it be argued that if one accepts *sāmānyalakṣaṇā* (the generic character of cognition), then once all objects of knowledge are known as "knowable" (*prameyatva*), it would result in omniscience; for even when all objects of knowledge have been known as "knowable," [omniscience does not follow].

Because there would be an absence of omniscience due to the non-cognition of all objects in their specific details; likewise, if the cognition-characterized [perception] (*jñānalakṣaṇā*) were not accepted, how could there be the cognition of fragrance in the cognition "fragrant sandalwood"? [The supernormal power] born of yoga (*yogaja*) is said to be of two kinds, according to the distinction between the "constantly engaged" (*yukta*) and the "intermittently engaged" (*yuñjāna*). (65) How could this be?

Although the manifestation of fragrance is possible even through general perception (*sāmānyalakṣaṇā*), nevertheless, the manifestation of the universal "fragrance-ness" (*saurabhatva*) occurs through cognition characterized by its own nature (*jñānalakṣaṇā*). Likewise, in cases where there is constant manifestation for one who is concentrated, there is another [type of perception] assisted by reflection (*cintā*); for instance, when a mass of dust is known as smoke.
The appearance of a mass of dust during its subsequent determination occurs through the "characteristic of knowledge" (*jñānalakṣaṇā*). Regarding the term "born of yoga" (*yogaja*):

the meaning is that it is a specific quality (*dharma*) produced by the practice of yoga, as propounded in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Purāṇas*, and so forth. Because there are two types of practitioners—those who are already united (*yukta*) and those who are currently practicing union (*yuñjāna*)—there are likewise two types of this quality.
The meaning is that there are two kinds [of knowledge]. Regarding the phrase "of one who is disciplined" (*yuktasya*):
for one who is disciplined, by means of the mind aided by the dharma born of yoga, there is at all times knowledge whose object is the entire range of categories, such as space, atoms, and so forth.

It must be that even a particular mental state (*cintāviśeṣa*) is a contributory cause for the second [instance]. Thus ends the first chapter, on Perception, in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.
Now, the section on inference (anumānakhaṇḍa):
The operation [of inference] is reflective cognition (parāmarśa), while the instrument (karaṇa) is the cognition of pervasion (vyāpti). In inference, that which is being known...
But the *liṅga* (the mark) is not the instrument (*karaṇa*). He explains inference (*anumiti*) as follows: "The operation (*vyāpāra*), however...

In inference—that is, in the act of inferring—the knowledge of pervasion (*vyāptijñāna*) is the instrument, and the *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection) is the operation. To illustrate: by a person who [has previously perceived] smoke in a kitchen or similar place...

The pervasion by fire has been previously apprehended; subsequently, that same person sees a streak of smoke with its base unbroken on a mountain or some other location. Immediately thereafter, he experiences a recollection of the pervasion in the form: "smoke is pervaded by fire. And after that...

The cognition "this [mountain] possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" is what is called *parāmarśa* (subsumptive reflection); immediately following that, the inference "the mountain is fiery" arises.

Regarding this, the ancient teachers maintain that the inferential mark (*liṅga*) known as being pervaded (*vyāpyatva*) is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inference, [even] by means of an inferential mark that is yet to come and so forth.

In that case, there would be no inference. (67) The cognition of the pervaded as residing in the subject is called *parāmarśa*. He refutes that [view] by stating "being known" (*jñāyamāna*). He provides the reasoning for the fact that the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not the instrument (*karaṇa*) of inference by saying "future and so forth" (*anāgatādi*). If [the mark were the instrument] in inference...

The inferential mark (liṅga) would be the instrument [of inference]; however, there could be no inference through a past or future inferential mark, because at that time the inferential mark—which is the instrument of inference—would be absent. ||66-67||

Regarding the phrase "of the pervaded" (*vyāpyasya*): the cause of inference is a cognition that apprehends the qualified relation between the subject (*pakṣa*) and that which is qualified by the pervasion (*vyāpti*). And this [cause] is either the cognition "the pervaded is in the subject" (*pakṣe vyāpyaḥ*) or the cognition "the subject possesses the pervaded" (*pakṣo vyāpyavān*). As for the inference itself, it arises from the cognition "the pervaded is in the subject" with respect to the subject.
From the cognition "the subject possesses the pervader" (vyāpyavān), there arises [the cognition] "the subject possesses the probandum" (sādhyavān).
Others hold that from both types of *parāmarśa*, the resulting inference is exclusively of the form "the subject possesses the probandum. Now, one might object:

Since it is observed that inference arises from two cognitions alone— namely, where there is first the perception "the mountain possesses smoke" and subsequently the recollection "smoke is pervaded by fire"— even without the cognition "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire," [it follows that] the cognition must be one that apprehends the qualified object as being qualified by the pervasion (*vyāpti*).

If it is argued that [inferential knowledge] is not the cause in all cases, but rather that being the cognition of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) under a mode delimited by the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka-prakāraka*) is necessarily the cause, and that postulating a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) in that regard involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), we say: no. For even when the delimitor of pervasion is unknown, there occurs the cognition: "This possesses what is pervaded by fire."

Because inference arises from knowledge [of pervasion], and for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the cause [of inference] is the knowledge of the property of being a locus (*pakṣadharmatā*) qualified by the mode of pervasion (*vyāpti*). Furthermore, an inference would otherwise arise from the cognition "the mountain possesses smoke," because there exists a knowledge of the property of being a locus qualified by the mode of smokeness (*dhūmatva*), which serves as the delimiting factor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*).

Nor should it be argued that the cause [of inference] is the knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatājñāna*) qualified by a qualifier that delimits the pervasion of what is being grasped; for if that were so, an inference would arise in Maitra from his knowledge of the presence of the reason in the subject, even though Caitra has grasped the pervasion. If...

If it is said that "the cognition of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatājñāna) for a particular person, having as its qualifier the delimitor of the pervasion (vyāpyatāvacchedaka) being grasped by that same person, is the cause for that person's inference," then there would be an infinite number of cause-and-effect relations. In my view, however, [the relation is] by way of inherence (samavāya).

The cognition of the property of the subject (pakṣadharmatā) as having pervasion (vyāpti) as its qualifier produces an inference through the relation of inherence (samavāya); thus, there is no infinite regress of causal relations. However, if it is asserted that the cognition of the property of the subject and the cognition of pervasion as its qualifier are independent causes, then [the following applies]: the cognition of the property of the subject as having pervasion as its qualifier...

If that which is independent [of other causes] is called the cause, then there would be two distinct relations of cause and effect; consequently, an inference would arise even from such cognitions as "smoke is pervaded by fire" and "the mountain possesses light. And thus, this would apply even in cases where there are two separate cognitions.

A distinct cognition must be postulated as the result, since complexity resulting from the perspective of the result is not a fault. The term "pervaded" (vyāpya) means the locus of pervasion (vyāptyāśraya).
To the question of what pervasion (vyāpti) is in that context, he says: "Pervasion.
In such cases as "there is fire because there is smoke," the fire is the probandum (sādhya), and the locus of the probandum is the pervasion.
"Non-connection [of the reason] with that which is other than the locus of the probandum (sādhyavada) is cited as the definition. (68) The kitchen and so forth are "other than that" (tadanya);

lakes and so forth are different from those, and the fact that smoke does not exist there constitutes the application of the definition. In cases such as "smoke-possessing [mountain] because of fire," [the locus of the probandum] is other than the heated iron ball and so forth.

There is no over-extension [of the definition] because of the existence of fire in the mountain (*vahni*). Here, it should be understood that by whichever relation the probandum (*sādhya*) exists, by that same relation the locus possessing the probandum (*sādhyavat*) is to be understood. Otherwise, since fire exists in the mountain by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), and its parts—such as the kitchen hearth (*mahānasa*) and so forth—are distinct from it, smoke would exist in those [parts].

Because [the definition] would be over-pervasive (*avyāpti*) due to the existence [of such a thing]. Furthermore, "other than that which possesses the probandum" (*sādhyavadanya*) should be understood as possessing a difference whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by the state of possessing the probandum (*sādhyavattvāvacchinna*). By this, there is no fault even if smoke exists on a mountain (*parvata*), etc., which is distinct from the kitchen (*mahānasa*), etc., which possesses some particular fire. By which...

The status of being a reason (hetutā) is to be understood through that very same relation; by this, it should be understood that [the reason] must be absent from what is other than that which possesses the probandum (sādhyavadanyāvṛttitva).

Therefore, there is no flaw even if smoke exists in a part of smoke—which is other than that which possesses the probandum—by way of the relation of inherence (samavāya). And as for the absence from what is other than that which possesses the probandum...

It is the absence whose counter-positive-ness is delimited by the property of "subsisting in something other than that which possesses the probandum" (*sādhyavadanyavṛttitvatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāvaḥ*). By this, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of "smoke-possessing [mountain] because of fire," even though there exists an absence of subsistence in things such as lakes—which are other than that which possesses the probandum. Here, although in cases such as "substance because of existence qualified by being other than quality and action," etc., [the definition applies].

Because the qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) and pure existence (*śuddhasattā*) are one and the same, there is no non-occurrence [of the reason] in things other than the locus of the probandum, such as quality (*guṇa*) and so forth; nevertheless, non-occurrence must be stated in terms of the delimiting factor of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedakarūpa*).
The resulting meaning is that the delimiting factor of the reasonhood is not a delimiting factor of the occurrence (*vṛttitānavacchedaka*).

68. Alternatively, pervasion (vyāpti) is said to be the co-occurrence (aikādhikaraṇya) of the reason with a probandum that is the counter-positive of an absence residing in the locus of the reason. 69. But surely, in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*) where the probandum is "knowability" (*jñeyatva*) and so forth, there is no pervasion because the counter-positive of the absence of the locus of the probandum is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Furthermore:

In cases such as "existence (sattā) [is] because of being a genus (jāti)," since it is unestablished that there is an occurrence in something other than the locus of the probandum—such as a universal (sāmānya)—by means of the delimiting relation of the reason, namely inherence (samavāya), he says:
"Alternatively... That which has its occurrence (vṛtti) residing in the possessor of the reason is so described.
Absence (*viraha*) means non-existence (*abhāva*).

Thus, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is said to be the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the probans with a probandum that is not the counter-positive (*apratiyogin*) of that absence which resides in the locus of the probans. In this regard, although there is fire on the mountain...

In cases such as "because of smoke" (*dhūmāt*), there is smoke in the mountain, which is the locus of the probans (*hetu*); since the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the absence residing in that locus (the mountain) is fire and so forth, there is an over-extension (*avyāpti*) [of the definition] to those fires.
Nor should it be argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) exists only between smoke and fire when they are co-locative (*samānādhikaraṇa*).

Furthermore, because the absence of both [the property and its counter-positive] exists even in the case of "otherness" (*anyatva*) and the like, there would be the cognition that "even when one is present, the pair does not exist"; thus, there would be an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "this possesses quality (*guṇa*), because it is a substance (*dravyatva*).
Nevertheless, that which is the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*) is the delimiting factor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*).

It must be stated that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is the co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) delimited by that [property]. Now, in such cases as "that which possesses a genus pervaded by *rūpatva* (colorness) is earth, because it is earth," the delimiters of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) are the genera pervaded by *rūpatva*; and of those, there are genera such as whiteness (*śuklatva*), and so forth.

If it is argued that there is an over-narrow definition (avyāpti) because the property of being the delimiting factor of the counter-correlativity of the absence of occurrence in a blue pot and the like exists [in the universal *rūpatva*], we say no; for in that case, what is the delimitor of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) is precisely the state of being a genus pervaded by *rūpatva*, through a mediated relation (*paramparayā*). Indeed, an absence delimited by such a property does not exist anywhere.
Because the cognition "there exists on the earth that which possesses a genus pervaded by *rūpatva* (the nature of color/form), and there does not exist [such a thing]" would result; for,

since pervasion (*vyāpti*) differs according to the difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and other factors, in such a case, the delimitor of the delimitor of the state of being the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedakatāvacchedaka*)— [The remainder of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]

Some also maintain that "that which is not the delimitant of the counter-positive-ness" alone constitutes the definition. Furthermore, the locus of the reason (*hetu*) must be understood as the locus qualified by the delimitant of the reasonhood (*hetutāvacchedaka*).
By this, in cases such as "Substance (dravya) [is] because of existence qualified by being other than quality and action," etc., [the definition is preserved].

Even though substanceness (*dravyatva*) is the counter-positive of an absence residing in its substratum—namely, pure existence (*śuddhasattā*)—there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). It should be understood that the locus of the reason (*hetu*) is determined by the relation that delimits the state of being a reason (*hetutāvacchedaka-sambandha*);
therefore, although [substancehood] is the counter-positive of an absence residing in the parts of smoke—which are loci of smoke by way of inherence (*samavāya*)—[this does not constitute a flaw].

There is no non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding the mountain (*vaḍabhi*). Furthermore, the absence (*abhāva*) should be understood as being "non-co-located with its counter-positive" (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*). By this, in the case of the inference "this [mountain] possesses monkey-contact because it is a tree," although the counter-positive of the absence of monkey-contact existing in this tree (delimited by its base) is indeed monkey-contact, there is no non-pervasion of monkey-contact. Nor is the state of being non-co-located with the counter-positive...
If [the definition] consists in "subsisting in a locus that is not the locus of the counter-positive," then there is likewise the same lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*);

for the absence that subsists in qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth—which are loci other than the locus of the counter-positive, namely the conjunction with a monkey—exists indeed in the tree, delimited by its root. However, if...

If it were defined as "not occurring in the locus of the counter-positive," then there would be over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in cases such as "this [mountain] possesses conjunction because it possesses existence" (*saṃyogī sattvāt*);

for the absence of conjunction in a quality (*guṇa*), which is a locus of existence, has its counter-positive residing in a substance (*dravya*), which is the locus of the reason (*hetu*). Thus it must be stated [that the definition applies only] to the locus of the reason.
Because what is intended is that which is not qualified by the property of residing in a locus other than the counter-positive's locus.

The refined definition is: "an absence that resides in the locus of the probans, where that locus is not the locus of its own counter-positive. [The term] "not being the locus of the counter-positive" [is explained as follows:]

Alternatively, it must be stated that [the locus] is not the substratum of that which is delimited by the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). By this, in cases such as "possessing qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) because of being a genus (*jāti*)," there is no fault, even though the quality (*guṇa*), which is the substratum of the genus (*jāti*), is the substratum of the existence (*sattā*) that is the counter-correlate of the absence of qualified existence. Here...

It should be understood that the non-locusness of the counter-positive (pratiyogī) is with respect to the relation that delimits the probandum-ness (sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha). By this, in cases such as "He possesses knowledge because of existence," there is no defect even though a pot—which is a locus of existence—is a locus of knowledge by way of the relation of objectivity (viṣayatā). And thus, [the definition holds] in cases such as "The mountain possesses fire because of smoke."
In the locus of smoke (*dhūmādhikaraṇa*), there is no deficiency even though there is an absence of fire (*vahniviraha*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*).

Now, [one might ask]: does it mean the non-locus-ness of any particular counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) delimited by the delimitor of counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), or rather the non-locus-ness of that [counter-positive] in its general form?
Alternatively, what is intended is the state of not being the locus of that which is delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of anything whatsoever.

In the first case, there is likewise an over-narrowness (avyāpti) in the inference "This [tree] possesses monkey-contact, because it is this-tree-ness," since [the absence of monkey-contact] is delimited by the delimitor of the counter-correlativity of the absence of monkey-contact.
Even the conjunction of a monkey with a tree-covering has as its locus a tree that is not the locus of that [conjunction].

In the second case, however, there is the non-establishment of an absence that is non-co-located with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇābhāvāprasiddhi*), because every absence whatsoever is co-located with its counter-positive, which consists of its own absence qualified by existence in the preceding moment.

Furthermore, in cases such as "there is fire because there is smoke," although the locus of the counter-positive— which consists of the absence of the pot itself qualified by its existence in the preceding moment—

is indeed the mountain and so forth (in the case of the absence of a pot), nevertheless, it remains true that the mountain is not the locus of that counter-positive with respect to the relation that delimits the probandumhood (*sādhyatāvacchedaka-sambandha*). How [then could there be a fallacy]?

It should not be argued that there is no instance of an absence whose locus is different from the locus of its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇābhāvāprasiddhi*). For, within the absence of fire (in a lake), there is the absence of a jar; since this absence of a jar is identical in nature to the absence of fire, fire is indeed the counter-positive of that absence of a jar, and its locus is the mountain and so forth—in this manner [the definition holds].
Because that which is non-coexistent with its counter-positive is unestablished. Even if it is argued that in the absence of a jar and so forth,

the absence of fire and so forth is distinct, nevertheless, there is a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases such as "that which possesses the absence of smoke has the absence of fire," for in that instance...

The delimiting relation of the probandum is the relation of identity (*svarūpasambandha*); by means of this, the locus of the reason possesses the locusness of its own counter-positive—which is the absence of that very absence—qualified by existence in the preceding moment. However, in the third [definition], there is under-extension (*avyāpti*) in cases such as "the self possesses the absence of conjunction with a monkey, because it is a self."
In that case, the self-existence (*ātma-vṛtti*) is the absence of the absence of conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyogābhāvābhāva*), which is conjunction with a monkey (*kapisaṃyoga*).
Since this is a quality (*guṇatva*), the delimitor of its counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) is also the state of being the general absence of qualities (*guṇasāmānyābhāvatva*).
Thus, the locus of the reason (*hetvadhikaraṇa*), namely the self, would not be a locus for that which is delimited by it. This is not so.

This is because what is intended [by the definition] is the non-qualification by such a counter-correlativity-limit (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) as that which does not reside in the locus of the reason (hetumat), being delimited by a counter-correlativity-limit of a certain kind. Now, consider the case: "Time possesses a jar, because of its temporal dimension" (kālo ghaṭavān kālaparimāṇāt).

There is the problem of the non-establishment of an absence that is non-co-located with its counter-positive; for Mahākāla, as the locus of the reason, being the substratum of the entire universe, every absence whatsoever has its counter-positive located within it by way of the temporal qualification relation (*kālika-viśeṣaṇatā*), which is the relation delimiting the probandum. Regarding this, some [object]:

The absence of a pot qualified by the difference from Great Time (*mahākāla*) is non-co-referential with its counter-positive (*pratiyogivyadhikaraṇa*) therein; for although Great Time is the locus of the pot, it is not the locus of a pot qualified by the difference from Great Time, because the difference from Great Time does not exist in Great Time. In reality, however:

By that relation, [the definition of non-contradiction consists in] the absence, in the generality of the counterpositivenesses of absences residing in the locus of the reason— which is not the locus of the counterpositive by way of the relation delimiting the counterpositiveness—
of both the property of being delimited by a particular relation and the property of being delimited by a particular attribute.
It should be understood that the pervasion of the cause by that which is delimited by that property [is what is meant].

And thus, in cases such as "Time possesses a jar, because of its dimension," even though the jar— which is the counter-positive of the absence of a jar in the relation of conjunction— is not present in the locus of the reason (the dimension), [it is nevertheless absent] in the locus of the reason.
When [the absence] exists at Mahākāla, that very absence of a jar—due to its conjunction—is present;

since there exists in the counter-positiveness (*pratiyogitā*) of that [absence] the absence of both the property of being delimited by the temporal relation (*kālikasaṃbandhāvaccchinnatva*) and the property of being delimited by jar-ness (*ghaṭatvāvaccchinnatva*), there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). Now, [consider the following case]: "There is fire possessing the property of being knowable (*prameyavahnimān*), because of smoke. In such cases...

If it is argued that "being delimited by a property larger than the object of inference" is unestablished because a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) cannot serve as a delimitor, we say no: where there exists no proof that is devoid of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), that is the subject (*pakṣa*); and from the cognition of [the reason's] subsistence therein, inferential knowledge arises.

The summary is as follows: because the cognition that "there is no [entity] possessing a conch-like neck and so forth" apprehends the counter-positiveness delimited by the property of possessing a conch-like neck and so forth, it is accepted that even a cumbersome property (*gurudharma*) can serve as a delimitor (*avacchedaka*). Regarding the phrase "subsistence in the subject" (*pakṣavṛttitva*): [text continues].

What is this "being a subject" (*pakṣatva*)? He says: "by the desire to prove" (*siṣādhayiṣayā*). The meaning is that the subject (*pakṣa*) is that which possesses the absence of proof qualified by the absence of the desire to prove;
the mere desire to prove is not the state of being a subject, for [the status of a subject] exists even without the desire to prove.

From the name "thundering cloud," one infers the existence of clouds; therefore, even doubt regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) does not constitute the state of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), because that inference occurs even without such doubt. Furthermore, even when certainty regarding the probandum exists, an inference indeed takes place provided there is a desire to prove it (*siṣādhayiṣā*). Therefore...

The absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) is a qualifier for "establishment" (*siddhi*). Thus, where there is no establishment, subjecthood (*pakṣatā*) exists provided there is a desire to prove, whether that desire is present or absent;
where there is a desire to prove, subjecthood exists whether there is establishment or not; and where there is both establishment and a desire to prove...

In that case, there is no absence of "pakṣatā" (the state of being a subject), because the established conclusion (*siddhi*) qualified by the absence of the desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) is present. Now, one might object: where an established conclusion arises immediately after the "parāmarśa" (subsumptive reflection), and subsequently the desire to prove arises, there would be no inference at the time of the desire to prove, because the *parāmarśa* has already perished. Where...

The desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), the inference-warranting consideration (*parāmarśa*), and the proof (*siddhi*) occur in succession. Among these, at the time of the desire to prove, the proof has already perished; therefore, inference arises solely due to the absence of an obstructing factor.
In a case where the desire to prove, the proof, and the inference-warranting consideration all occur, the desire to prove no longer exists at the time of the inference-warranting consideration.

If it is argued that in other cases as well—such as at the time of accomplishment (*siddhi*) or at the time of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—there is no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), because simultaneous existence of qualities residing in the same substratum is prohibited, then how can "being qualified by the absence of the desire to prove" be a qualification of accomplishment? [The answer is: It is not so, because where...

From the perception or recollection that "the mountain possesses smoke not pervaded by fire" [i.e., smoke from a kitchen], there arises the desire to prove [the presence of fire]; in that case, because of the necessity of including that qualification for the fulfillment of the status of being a subject (*pakṣatā*), this [qualification] is required. However, this...

The object of cognition (*bodhya*): *Pakṣatā* (the state of being the subject) with respect to an inference characterized by a particular logical mark (*liṅga*) is the absence of a proof (*siddhi*), qualified by the absence of a desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*) of that same kind as exists whenever there is a proof. Therefore, when there is both a proof and a subsumptive reflection (*parāmarśa*), whatever [other] cognition may exist—

Even when there is a desire such as "let [inferential knowledge] arise," no inference occurs. However, when there is the perceptual cognition "the mountain possesses smoke which is pervaded by fire" and "the mountain possesses fire," if there is a desire for a cognition other than perception—such as "let a cognition distinct from perception arise"—then [inference] indeed occurs. Likewise, when there is the consideration of smoke (*dhūmaparāmarśa*), [inference occurs] through light (*āloka*).
Even when there is a desire such as "I wish to infer the mountain's possession of fire," no inference occurs.

It must be stated that, at a time when there is no desire to prove (*siṣādhayiṣā*), a specific instance of established knowledge (*siddhi*)—in the presence of which no inference occurs—is precisely what acts as the inhibitor of that particular inference. By this [principle],...
Even though there is the cognition "the mountain is fiery, made of stone, and increasing," there is no contradiction with the inference; however,
this is so even when the probandum is established as being co-locational (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the delimiting factor of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Since it is observed that there is no inference with respect to that [specific] delimitation, mere *siddhi* (the state of being already known) is the opponent to an inference delimited by the *pakṣatāvacchedaka* (the delimitor of the subject). However, this must be noted: where, immediately after a doubt such as "Is this a person or not?", there arises the cognition "This possesses hands and so forth, which are pervaded by personhood."
In that case, when there is no desire to infer (*anumitsā*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) occurs for a person and not inference;

therefore, the causal complex for perception (*pratyakṣasāmagrī*)—qualified by the absence of the desire to infer and having the same object—is an independent inhibitor, just like the desire to know a beautiful woman (*kāminījijñāsā*). Thus...
Because perception of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth does not arise immediately after the ascertainment (*parāmarśa*) without a desire for perception,
the causal complex for inference (*anumiti-sāmagrī*)— qualified by the absence of the desire for perception— is the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
the contradictory (*viruddha*), the unestablished (*asiddha*), the counter-balanced (*pratipakṣita*), and the one whose application is mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

And fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are of five kinds. In brief, [the knowledge of] a perception whose object is different [from the reason's object] is an inhibitor [of inference]. Following the discussion on the reason (*hetu*), he classifies the fallacious reasons, beginning with "inconstant" (*anaikāntika*).
Its definition, however, is that which—by virtue of having such-and-such an object—[renders inference impossible].
The nature of a defect (*doṣa*) is its being an obstacle to inferential cognition (*anumiti*).

To explain: defects are so called because they obstruct inferential cognition by virtue of having as their object [the fallacies of] inconstancy (*vyabhicāra*) and the like. And "having as its object" means "having as its object a specific qualified entity" (*yādṛśaviśiṣṭaviṣayakatva*). By this—

Even if the error regarding sublation (*bādhabhrama*) were to constitute an obstacle to inference, there would be no harm; for in that case, since the qualified entity "the mountain possesses the absence of fire" is unestablished (*aprasiddha*), it does not constitute a defect in the logical reason (*hetudoṣa*). Nor [is there a problem] at the time of the reflective cognition (*parāmarśa*) "it possesses the nature of being stony, which is pervaded by the absence of fire."

It should not be argued that there would be no fallaciousness (ābhāsatva) regarding smoke that does not pervade fire, because in that case the qualified [subject], namely "the locus possesses the absence of fire-pervaded [smoke]," is unestablished (aprasiddha); for such an objection is acceptable (iṣṭāpatti). Otherwise, it would follow that sublation (bādha) is a non-eternal defect.

Therefore, at the time of the *parāmarśa* "that [mountain] possesses stoniness which is pervaded by the absence of fire," the smoke—which is pervaded by fire—is not fallacious; there is merely an obstruction to inference due to error, but the reason (*hetu*) itself is not defective. And thus, [the definition of a fallacious reason is] that which exists in a locus possessing the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavadvṛtti-hetu*), and so forth.

The moderns (navyāḥ) maintain that a defect (*doṣa*) consists in its being related to the reason (*hetu*) by any relation whatsoever, and "being possessed of that" (*tadvattvam*) means having that [defect] as its property.

Regarding the term *para* (the other): the state of being a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsatva*) is the possession of that object (*viṣaya*) which, by virtue of being the content of a cognition, constitutes an obstacle to inference (*anumiti-virodhitva*). In the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), it is precisely the contradictory pervasion (*virodhivyāpti*) and so forth that functions in this way; and "being possessed of that" refers to the possession of such [contradictory pervasion].

[The definition applies] by way of a relation consisting in being a cognition [of that sublation]. And it is not the case that, in an instance such as "the mountain possesses fire because of smoke," the erroneous cognition of a sublation (bādhavibhrama) regarding the subject (pakṣa)— which, by virtue of having the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) as its object, constitutes an obstacle to inference— would also render that reason fallacious,
since that [subject] would likewise possess that [absence] by way of a relation consisting in being a cognition.

It should not be said that there is the consequence of [the reason] being sublated (*bādhitatva*). For in that case (in the case of a contradictory reason), no relation to the cognition is postulated;

whereas here, such a relation is postulated because of the conventional usage "it is counterbalanced" (*satpratipakṣita*), and in that case (in the case of a sublated reason), it is postulated because of the conventional usage "it is sublated" (*bādhita*).

They say [it is so] because of the absence of empirical usage (*vyavahāra*). Furthermore, being an opponent to inference (*anumiti*) means being an opponent to either the inference itself or its instrument (*tatkaraṇa*); by this, there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of a fallacious reason (*vyabhicārin*). And the cognition of a defect (*doṣajñāna*) is an obstacle to the inference produced by that very reason which is the object of that cognition.

Therefore, even though the cognition of deviation (vyabhicāra) does not constitute an obstacle to inference— since an inference can arise through another reason when there is a cognition of deviation regarding one reason, and since such a cognition of deviation does not apprehend the absence of that [other] reason— there is no harm [to our position].

Summary: According to the nature of the probandum (sādhya), the subject (pakṣa), and the reason (hetu), the inconclusive (anaikāntika) reason is of three kinds: the first is the common (sādhāraṇa), the other is the uncommon (asādhāraṇaka), and likewise the non-conclusive (anupasaṃhārī).
Whatever defects exist in the subject and the reason, the state of being "one or the other" of those [defects] constitutes [the inconclusiveness] therein.

The state of being a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsatva*). The mention of "fivefoldness" is intended with reference to the possible locations where such fallacies occur. Thus, *anaikāntika* (inconclusiveness) consists in being any one of the [three types], beginning with the *sādhāraṇa*. The *sādhāraṇa* is that which subsists in what is other than the locus of the probandum (*sādhyavat*); by means of this, the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is obstructed. The *asādhāraṇa*...

The reason (*hetu*) that does not share the same locus as the probandum (*sādhya*) prevents the apprehension of its co-locus with the probandum. Others, however, hold that the uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason] is that which does not occur in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), and that the similar instance is that which possesses the probandum as a certainty; and thus...

They state that in cases such as "Sound is non-eternal because it has the nature of sound" (*śabdo 'nityaḥ śabdatvāt*), when there is certainty regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) of the reason (*hetu*) because the reason is certain therein. Furthermore, the "non-conclusive" (*anupasaṃhārī*) [reason] is that whose probandum is not the counter-positive of an absolute absence (*atyantābhāvāpratiyogi*), and so forth; by this—

The apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is obstructed. However, the contradictory reason (*viruddha*), being the counter-positive of the absence that pervades the probandum (*sādhyavyāpaka*), acts as an obstacle by virtue of being the causal complex for the apprehension of the absence of the probandum. In the case of a counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), however, the opposing reason is the establisher of the absence of the probandum.

In this case, the distinction is that there is only one reason (*hetu*); specifically, a reason that establishes the absence of the probandum (*sādhyābhāva*) is presented as if it were a reason establishing the probandum. Furthermore, it is a "distinction" because it brings about the presence of a specific incapacity. A counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*) is a subject (*pakṣa*) which possesses that which is pervaded by the absence of the probandum.

Others hold that [the object of doubt] is the object of a presentation of its being possessed of a pervader of its absence—wherein the non-validity has not been apprehended—at a time when there is a presentation of its being possessed of a pervader of the probandum, wherein the non-validity has not been apprehended.
And in this case, the result is the mutual obstruction of inference due to the cognition of possession of a pervader of each other's absence. On this point, some say as follows:

Just as when there is contact between the eye and a jar, the cognition of the presence of a jar arises even though there is a cognition of the possession of the property pervaded by the absence of the jar;

and just as, even when there is the cognition of the conch-shell possessing the property of "conch-ness" which is pervaded by the absence of yellowness, the cognition "the conch is yellow" arises due to a defect such as jaundice— so too it is when both properties pervading the two alternatives are perceived.

Just as doubt arises in the form of perception regarding two alternatives, so too in the case of a counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*), there indeed occurs an inference in the form of doubt. However, where there is the observation of the pervader (*vyāpya*) of one alternative, no doubt arises because the manifestation of the second alternative is obstructed by its superior strength; this is established by the force of the observed result.
And they say that the state of being "possessing greater strength" or "possessing equal strength" is thus postulated. That is not correct;

for when there is a cognition of something possessing a property pervaded by the absence of that [object], there is no arising of a specific mental presentation (*upanītabhāna*), verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), or the like, with respect to that [object]. This is because [such arising] occurs only in the case of a cognition that is not produced by ordinary sense-contact and is not produced by a specific defect.

Its status as an impediment [to inference] is due to parsimony (*lāghava*), and not because there is a separate impediment for the specific case of "presented cognition" (*upanītabhāna*) or for verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*); this is because such a view would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Thus, since the impediment is present, how can there be an inference? For it is not as in the case of perception through ordinary sensory contact (*laukikasannikarṣa*).

In a case of counter-balanced opposition (*satpratipakṣa*), an inference in the form of doubt is epistemically valid, such that [the definition of inference] must be qualified by being distinct from such an inference. Furthermore, where there is a cognition of the locus as possessing the pervaders of both alternatives, doubt arises there because of the cognition of invalidity regarding both; it does not arise otherwise, for only that which has its invalidity ungrasped [leads to certainty].

[This is] because a contradictory cognition acts as an impediment. Non-establishment (*asiddhi*), however, consists in being any one of the types beginning with the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*).

The non-establishment of the locus is the absence of the locus-determinant (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). For example, where it is sought to be proven that "the golden mountain possesses fire," there [the mountain] is not...

When the knowledge "it consists of gold" exists, the result is the obstruction of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) regarding a mountain consisting of gold. As for the "unestablished nature of the essential form" (*svarūpāsiddhi*), it is the absence of that which is intended to be the pervader (*vyāpyatvābhimata*) in the subject (*pakṣa*). And in that regard, in cases such as "the lake is a substance because of smoke," [there is an absence] in the subject of that which is intended to be the pervader.

When the absence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) is known, the result is the obstruction of the "consideration" (*parāmarśa*), which consists in the knowledge that the subject possesses a reason pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*). As for cases such as the non-establishment of the probandum (*sādhyāprasiddhi*), they are included within the category of the unestablished nature of the pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*). Regarding the probandum...

The non-existence of the delimiting property of the probandum (*sādhyatāvacchedaka*) constitutes the "unestablishedness of the probandum" (*sādhyāprasiddhi*). When this [non-existence] is known, the result is the obstruction of the inferential consideration (*parāmarśa*) of the probandum as qualified by its delimiting property, in cases such as "the mountain possesses a golden fire. Likewise...

The absence of the delimiting property of the reason (*hetutāvacchedaka*) in the reason itself is the "unestablishedness of the probans" (*sādhanāprasiddhi*), as in the case of "because of smoke made of gold" and so forth. Here,

due to the absence of the cognition of the reason as qualified by its delimiting property, there is an absence of the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and other such cognitions based upon that [reason].

The result [of this definition] is as follows: in cases such as "blue smoke" (nīladhūma) and so forth, some maintain that because the property of being blue smoke (nīladhūmatva) is cumbersome (gurutayā), its failure to serve as a delimitor of the probans (hetutānavacchedakatvam) also constitutes the fallacy of unestablished pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi). As for sublation (bādha), it consists in the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva) in the subject (pakṣa); its result, however, is the obstruction of inferential cognition (anumitipratibandha).

The certainty regarding the absence of a property in a given locus is an opponent only to any cognition of that property in that same locus which is not produced by ordinary sensory contact and is not produced by some specific defect;
it is not, however, an opponent to a cognition that is common to doubt regarding the locus.

It is logical that the cognition of the connection between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the subject is the cause of inference, and that sublation (*bādha*) and the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*) constitute fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) by virtue of being contradictory to that [cognition]. This is because an inference with an unestablished probandum would not otherwise arise, and because inference occurs even without a doubt regarding the probandum and so forth. Thus, it is the same in the case of the cognition of the non-existence of the probandum.

Furthermore, the cognition of truth (*prāmāṇyajñāna*) is not an impediment [to inference], because there is no evidence for it and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Otherwise, even in cases such as a counter-balanced argument (*satpratipakṣa*), the cognition of the absence of the pervader (*tadabhāvavyāpyavattājñāna*) would result in being an impediment simply by virtue of having truth as its object.
Rather, what constitutes an impediment is a sublated cognition (*bādhadhī*) that is not overridden by a cognition of falsity (*bhramatvajñāna*). In that regard:

The knowledge of validity (*prāmāṇyajñāna*) is useful in some cases for dispelling the suspicion of error. Nor should it be argued that in a case of sublation (*bādha*), if the reason (*hetu*) exists in the subject (*pakṣa*), there is an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*), whereas if the reason is absent in the subject, the fault is simply the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*). This is because the cognition of sublation...

Because it is distinct from the cognition of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and so forth. Furthermore, in a case where a sublation-cognition (*bādhabuddhi*) arises immediately after the consideration (*parāmarśa*), since the cognition of deviation and the like are ineffective there, it must be stated that sublation is the inhibitor of inference. Likewise, in a case where there is a cognition of earthness as being pervaded by smell with respect to a jar delimited by its moment of origination—

In that case, it must be stated that sublation (*bādha*) alone functions as the impediment. Nor should it be asked how there can be sublation given that odor exists in the jar, which is the subject (*pakṣa*);
for it is established by experience that inference occurs with respect to the specific place and time delimited by the locus-determiner (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).

Those fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) that are distinct from those pervaded by sublation (*bādha*)— even if they are themselves pervaded by it— are included within that very category, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of an excess of fallacious reasons.
However, the counter-balanced reason (*satpratipakṣa*), which is pervaded by sublation, was treated as entirely distinct by the Sage who acts according to his own independent will.

The meaning of the section is that because it is taught separately, a reason that is pervaded by a counter-thesis is not an obstructer [of the inference]. ||71||72|| As for "that which is a similar instance" (*sapakṣa*):

that which exists in both the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is the "common" (*sādhāraṇa*) [inconclusive] reason; whereas that which is excluded from both is [the "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) inconclusive reason].

It is considered common to all beings (satvasādhāraṇa). Likewise, that which has no exclusion [from the subject] and has only positive concomitance (kevalānvayin) as its locus is also [so considered]. The meaning is that "common" (sādhāraṇa) refers to that which exists in both the similar instance (sapakṣa) and the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa). A similar instance (sapakṣa) is that in which the probandum (sādhya) is ascertained; a dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is...

"Different from that which possesses the probandum" (*sādhyavadbhinna*). The phrase "presence in the similar instance" (*sapakṣavṛttitvam*) is stated in order to exclude the contradictory reason (*viruddha*). In reality, however, "presence in the dissimilar instance" (*vipakṣavṛttitvam*) alone should be stated; for even though the contradictory reason shares the same character as the common (*sādhāraṇa*) reason, its status is distinct because the grounds for its being a defeater (*dūṣakatābīja*) are different. As for the phrase "that which is excluded from both": it is excluded from both the similar and the dissimilar instances.

Thus, the *itara* (the other) is the subject (*pakṣa*). The *sapakṣa* (similar instance) is that which is ascertained as possessing the property to be proven (*sādhyavat*). The *vipakṣa* (dissimilar instance) is that which is ascertained as being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyaśūnya*). In cases such as "Sound is impermanent because it possesses the nature of sound" (*śabdo 'nityaḥ śabdatvāt*), when there is doubt regarding impermanence in sound, then the status of being a *sapakṣa* belongs only to jars and the like, while it is excluded from sound itself.

And when it is "sound-ness," then that [reason] is uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). But when there is a certainty of impermanence regarding sound, then it is not uncommon. This, however, is the opinion of the ancients;
the view of the new school has already been stated [previously]. [Regarding the term] "purely positive" (*kevalānvayin*): "all is denotable."

In cases such as "because it is knowable" (*prameyatvāt*), since everything is the subject (*pakṣa*), there is no inference because there is no other locus for grasping concomitance (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, this is not correct, because there is no deficiency even if the concomitance is grasped in only one part of the subject. Or, let it be so.

The non-apprehension of concomitance (sahacāra) does not, by that much alone, constitute the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (ajñānarūpāsiddhi), nor does it constitute the status of being a pseudo-reason (hetvābhāsa).

That which does not exist at all in the locus of the probandum (sādhyavat) is declared to be the "contradictory" (viruddha) reason. First, there would be the unestablishedness of the locus (āśrayāsiddhi);
then, the unestablishedness of the essential nature (svarūpāsiddhi); and another is the unestablishedness of pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi).

Therefore, non-establishment (asiddhi) is threefold. (75) Non-establishment of the locus (pakṣāsiddhi) occurs where the locus would be, for example, "the mountain consists of jewels" or "the lake possesses smoke because it is a substance. Here, there is another [type of] non-establishment. (76) Another is non-establishment of the pervasion (vyāpyatvāsiddhi), which occurs in cases such as "blue smoke"; nevertheless, that [reason] has a probandum (sādhya) that is purely positive (kevalānvayi).

The term "tattva" has been explained. Regarding the phrase "that which possesses the probandum": by means of the particle *eva*, the absence of the reason (*hetu*) is indicated as being delimited by the possession of the probandum (*sādhyavattva*). Thus, its meaning is "being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the probandum. (74) He divides the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*): "unestablishedness of the locus," and so forth.

"Non-establishment of the locus" (pakṣāsiddhi) means non-establishment of the substratum (āśrayāsiddhi). "The others" means non-establishment of the essential nature (svarūpāsiddhi). Regarding "blue smoke and so forth": the property of being blue smoke and the like, due to its complexity (gurutva), cannot serve as the delimiting factor of the probans (hetutāvacchedaka).

Satpratipakṣa (counter-inference) occurs when there is a consideration (*parāmarśa*) of two contradictory reasons that are not composed of any other property that serves as a delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpyatāvacchedaka*) co-extensive with themselves. [In the definition], the term "co-extensive with itself" (*svasamānādhikaraṇa*) is included in order to include the state of being the prior absence of smoke (*dhūmaprāgabhāvatva*), because it is a delimitor of pervasion. The phrase "of two contradictory [reasons]" (*viruddhayoḥ*) [is used].

Even when there is a consideration (*parāmarśa*) of that which possesses a pervader of both the conjunction with smoke and its absence, there is no "counter-balanced opposition" (*satpratipakṣa*). Therefore, that in which the subject (*pakṣa*) is devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*) is cited as "sublation" (*bādha*). This occurs where properties such as odor are being proved for a jar at the time of its production. It was stated [previously] regarding two contradictory [reasons]. Thus, the object of a consideration of that which possesses a pervader of the probandum, occurring at the same time as a consideration of that which possesses a pervader of the absence of the probandum—which is contradictory to its own probandum—[is what constitutes sublation].

This is the meaning. "Devoid of the probandum" (sādhyaśūnya) means the subject (pakṣa) as qualified by the delimitor of the subjecthood (pakṣatāvacchedaka). By this, there is no defect even if odor exists in a jar. The same should be understood in the case of the statement: "The tree, delimited by its root, is in contact with a monkey. 75–76.
77 || 78 || Thus ends the section on inference (*anumāna-khaṇḍa*) in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by the venerable Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.
In the section on comparison (upamiti), first, when a villager sees a gavaya or similar animal for the first time, there arises a cognition of its similarity to a cow or other such animals.

It may be considered the instrument [of knowledge]. He explains analogy (*upamiti*)—starting with "of the villager": where some forest-dweller has told a villager, "The *gavaya* is denoted by the word 'gavaya' because it is similar to a cow," and subsequently, the villager [sees it] somewhere in the forest or elsewhere.
The gavaya is perceived; the observation of its similarity to a cow that arises therein is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of the analogy.

Immediately thereafter, the recollection of the meaning of the analogical statement—that "the gavaya is denoted by the word *gavaya* because it is similar to a cow"—is the operation (*vyāpāra*). Following that, [the cognition] "the gavaya is the referent of the term" arises from that analogical statement.
Recollection is said to be the [resulting] operation; however, the cognition of the word-potency for terms such as "gavaya" is the fruit of comparison.
The cognition that arises as "this is the denotation of the word *gavaya*" is *upamiti* (analogical knowledge);

however, the cognition "this [specific individual] is the denotation of the word *gavaya*" is not *upamiti*, because it would follow that there could be no apprehension of the word's power (*śakti*) with respect to other *gavayas*. || 79 || 80 || Thus.
The Section on Analogy from the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī* composed by Śrī Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya.
In the section on words (śabdakhaṇḍa), verse 4: Word-knowledge is the instrument; therein, the cognition of word-meanings is the intermediate operation; and verbal comprehension is the result.

The cognition of the word's capacity (*śaktidhī*) is the auxiliary cause. [The author] demonstrates the manner of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) with the words "But the cognition of the word" (*padajñānaṃ tu*). However, the word as being currently cognized is not the instrument (*karaṇa*), because verbal comprehension occurs even in the absence of a word, such as in the case of a silent verse (*mauniśloka*) and so forth. [He states] "the cognition of the word-meaning" (*padārthadhī*).

The operation (*vyāpāra*) is the recollection of the word-meaning produced by the word. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of verbal cognition even when the meaning of a word is presented through perception or other means to one who already possesses knowledge of that word. In this context as well, it should be understood that "being produced by the word" occurs through its *vṛtti* (denotative function); otherwise, [if this were not required], from words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), etc.,...
If the remembrance of space (*ākāśa*) were to arise through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), it would follow that space itself would be the object of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*).

Furthermore, "function" (*vṛtti*) is a relation consisting of either denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). It is precisely here that the knowledge of denotation is required; for if the denotation has not been previously apprehended, even when there is the cognition of the word, [verbal cognition does not occur].

Because memory of that [object] does not arise through a connection with that [word]. For the cognition of a word brings the word-meaning to mind by way of being the cognition of one related member of a relation. And the power (śakti) is the relation between the word and the word-meaning; and that [power] consists in [the fact that] "from this word, this meaning is to be understood."

Thus, the traditional view (saṃpradāya) holds that there is indeed a primary denotative power (śakti) in a name based on the will of God (īśvarecchā), because the will of God exists in the form "on the eleventh day, the father shall give a name"; however, there is no such power in a name established by modern convention. The Neo-Naiyāyikas (navyāḥ), however, maintain that the will of God is not the denotative power, but rather the desire itself (icchā).

Therefore, they say that even in the case of a modern convention, there is indeed *śakti* (denotative power). The apprehension of this power (*śaktigraha*), however, arises from grammar and other sources. For it is said: "The elders declare that the apprehension of *śakti* comes from grammar, comparison, lexicons, the speech of trustworthy persons, usage, the remainder of a sentence, explicit explanation (*vivṛti*), and the proximity of a word whose meaning is already established. [This applies] to verbal roots, bases, suffixes, and so forth.

The apprehension of word-meaning (śaktigraha) arises from grammar; however, in some cases, it is abandoned when there is a subverting factor (bādhaka). For example, grammarians maintain that the expressive power (śakti) of a verb resides in the agent. In sentences such as "Caitra cooks" (caitraḥ pacati), there is a coreferential relation (abhedānvaya) between Caitra and the agent. But that [view] is abandoned due to the fault of complexity (gaurava). Rather, [the power resides in the action].

The meaning of the suffix *kṛt* is the effort (*kṛti*), because of parsimony. And this effort appears as a qualifier (*prakārībhūya*) in relation to Caitra and others. Nor should it be argued that, since the agent is not denoted, the third case ending would follow after the word "Caitra";
for in that regard, the non-denotation of the agent's number is the governing factor. And that which is capable of denoting number [is what determines the case ending].
[The referent] is that which is not subsumed under [grammatical roles] such as *karman* (object) and is presented by a word ending in the first case (*prathamāvibhakti*).

The meaning of the phrase "such as *karman*" is: being outside the scope of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) as a qualifier of anything else. Consequently, in examples such as "Maitra goes like Caitra," there is no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) of number with Caitra. Where...

The phrase "ending in the nominative case" (*prathamānta*) is included to exclude cases where there is no intention to qualify the object of the action (*karma-ādi*) and so forth. Alternatively, the meaning of the first part [of the definition] is "not being a qualifier of anything other than the meaning of the verbal root. By this, in the sentence "Maitra goes like Caitra," Caitra and others are excluded. This also applies in cases such as "he cooks slightly" (*stokaṃ pacati*).

The second part [of the definition] is for the purpose of excluding [the denotation of] "a little" (*stoka*) and so forth; its exclusion is because that [denotation] is presented by a word ending in the second case (*dvitīyā*). Likewise, there is no expressive power (*śakti*) in the operation (*vyāpāra*), due to the [resulting] complexity (*gaurava*). However, in cases such as "the chariot goes" (*ratho gacchati*), [the meaning is either] the operation or the substratum (*āśrayatva*).

In cases such as *jānāti* ("he knows"), there is a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) regarding the locus (*āśrayatva*); however, in cases such as *naśyati* ("it perishes"), it refers to the counter-positive (*pratiyogitva*). How the apprehension of power (*śaktigraha*) occurs through comparison (*upamāna*) has already been explained. Likewise, the apprehension of power also arises from lexicons (*kośa*). This is occasionally set aside when there is a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), as in the case of words like *nīla* ("blue") with respect to blue color and so forth.

Furthermore, although the lexicon teaches that the word’s denotative power (*śakti*) resides in that which is qualified by "blue," nevertheless, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the power resides in "blue" and so forth alone; rather, it is through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) that the power applies to that which is qualified by "blue" and so forth.
The same applies to the testimony of a reliable person (*āptavākya*); for example, [the statement] "The cuckoo is denotable by the word *pika*."

From words such as "pika" and so forth, the apprehension of the word-potency (*śakti*) occurs with respect to the cuckoo; likewise, it occurs through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). For example, when an elder who is the instigator (*prayojaka-vṛddha*) says, "Bring the jar," and the elder who is the prompted agent (*prayojya-vṛddha*) hears that and brings the jar, a child standing nearby observes this act of bringing the jar.

He determines that the action [expressed by] "bring the jar" is prompted by the utterance of the word. Then, through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*āpoddhāra*) regarding sentences such as "bring the jar" and "lead the cow," he grasps the denotative power (*śakti*) of words like "jar" as residing in objects such as jars that are conjoined with an action to be accomplished (*kāryānvita*). And thus, [in the case of the sentence] "there is a blue jar on the ground"...

Some maintain that because of such words [as "it is"] there is no verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), since the capacity of words like "jar" is determined only with respect to the cognition of a jar as connected to an action (*kārya*), and because the optative suffixes (*liṅ*) and so forth have capacity toward the cognition of "taskness" (*kāryatā*); thus, in their absence, there is no verbal cognition. This is not correct.

Even though the capacity [of words] is initially determined with respect to objects such as a jar as connected with an action (*kāryānvita*), it is appropriate to subsequently abandon that [interpretation] for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). For this very reason, in cases such as "A son has been born to you, O Caitra" or "Your daughter is pregnant," pleasure and pain are understood through the brightening or darkening of the face.

Having inferred that [the cognition] has that [sentence] as its cause by means of the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), and having determined it to be verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*), one ascertains that word as its cause. Thus, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*), there is no expressive power (*śakti*) in [the word] with respect to an object associated with an action (*kāryānvita*). Nor should another word such as "see him" (*taṃ paśya*) be supplied there, for there is no evidence; for instance, in the case of "Caitra, a son is born to you."

And because [the word] "born" or "dead" and so forth do not apply there; thus, by parsimony (*lāghava*), having abandoned the assumption of a denotative power (*śakti*) for the word "jar" in the sense of a jar as connected with other factors, one determines that the word "jar" has its power restricted to the jar alone. In this way, the apprehension of power also occurs through supplementary statements (*vākyaśeṣa*); for example, in the case of the statement, "The sacrificial oblation (*caru*) consists of barley (*yava*)," regarding the word "barley."

The noble ones (āryas) employ the term *dīrghaśūka* for a specific type of grain, whereas the barbarians (*mlecchas*) use the term *kaṅgu*. For it is said: "Then while other plants wither, these remain rejoicing; in spring, the birth of all crops occurs."

From the remainder of the sentence, "And the barley grains stand rejoicing, adorned with ears," the capacity [of the word *yava*] is determined to reside in long-awned barley (*dīrghaśūka*); however, its use for *kaṅgu* (paspalum scrobiculatum) arises from a misconception regarding that capacity. This is because it would be cumbersome to postulate multiple capacities. But in the case of words such as *hari* (lion/horse), etc.,...

Because there is no decisive evidence [to the contrary], one must assume multiple powers [of words]. Likewise, the apprehension of power occurs through *vivaraṇa* (explanation). *Vivaraṇa*, however, is the explanation of the meaning of a word by means of another word having the same meaning;
for example, from the explanation of "the jar exists" (*ghaṭo 'sti*) by "the pot exists" (*kalaśo 'sti*), the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*) [is understood to have the power] in the sense of "pot."

The apprehension of word-meaning (*śaktigraha*) occurs as follows: from the analysis (*vivaraṇa*) of "he cooks" (*pacati*) by means of "he performs cooking" (*pākaṃ karoti*), it is inferred that the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) has "effort" (*yatna*) as its meaning. Likewise, the apprehension of word-meaning also arises from the proximity of a well-known word (*prasiddhapada*). For example, in such cases as: "Here, on this mango tree, the *pika* bird sings sweetly."

Regarding the statement that the apprehension of the denotative power (*śakti*) of the word *pika* occurs with respect to the cuckoo: some hold that the apprehension of the power resides in the genus (*jāti*) alone and not in the individual (*vyakti*), because [the relation] would otherwise be erratic and because there are infinite individuals; yet, they argue that since the manifestation of the genus is impossible without the individual, the individual is also manifested. This is not correct. [The reason is that] the power...

Because the manifestation of the individual (vyakti) would otherwise be impossible; nor is there a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) regarding the individual, since the cognition of the individual occurs even without the recognition of such an impossibility; nor is there an infinite number of powers (śakti), because a single power is admitted for all individuals.

Nor is there a lack of pervasion (ananugama), because it is precisely the genus (gotva) and so forth that serves as the pervader. Furthermore, if the apprehension of the expressive power (śaktigraha) is "the cow is the denotable," then the power resides in the individual (vyakti). But if the apprehension of the expressive power is "the genus (gotva) is the denotable," then there arises a recollection of the object having the genus as its qualifier (prakāra), and subsequently the verbal cognition (śābdabodha).

It would not be so, because the recollection of the word-meaning—which arises from the knowledge of the expressive power (*śakti*) through having a common mode of presentation—is a cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, if the expressive power resides in "cowness" (*gotva*), then "cowness-ness" (*gotvatva*) must be stated as the delimiting factor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*). But what is this "cowness-ness"?

[The definition of *gotva* is] being inherent in all cows while not being inherent in anything other than cows. And thus, because individual cows (*go-vyakti*) enter into the delimiting factor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), there is indeed heaviness (*gaurava*) for you.

Therefore, since it is impossible to account for the cognition of those respective individuals as qualified by their respective universals (*jāti*) and forms (*ākṛti*), the denotative power (*śakti*) that must be postulated resides in the individual itself as qualified by its universal and form.

It is said that [a word] "rests" [upon its meaning]. A word is capable [of conveying meaning], and it is of four kinds: in some cases etymological (*yaugika*), in some cases conventional (*rūḍha*), in some cases both etymological and conventional (*yogarūḍha*), and in some cases both etymological and conventional by way of a single form (*yaugikarūḍha*). To illustrate: where only the meaning of the constituent parts is understood, that is etymological, such as the word *pācaka* ("cook") and others. Where [the meaning is understood] independently of the power of the constituent parts...

That which is apprehended through the power of the whole (samudāya-śakti) is *rūḍha* (conventional); for example, words such as *gomaṇḍala*. However, where the power of the whole also exists within the scope of the power of the parts (*avayava-śakti*), that is *yogarūḍha* (etymological-conventional); for example, the word *paṅkaja*. To explain: the word *paṅkaja*, by the power of its parts—

It conveys the meaning of the agent of the production of mud through its collective power (*samudāya-śakti*), and it conveys the lotus as such (in the form of *padmatva*) through its collective power. Nor should it be argued that there would be usage for the water-lily (*kumuda*) by means of the individual component powers (*avayava-śakti*) alone; for when there is knowledge of a conventional term (*rūḍha*), there is no cognition of a purely etymological (*yaugika*) meaning.

The ancients [hold] that it is because [the word "lotus"] acts as an obstacle [to the application of the component meaning]. In reality, however, when the lotus is presented through the power of the whole (samudāya-śakti), the meaning of the components—the agent of the act of producing mud—becomes connected [to it] due to proximity. But where the sublation of the conventional meaning (rūḍhi-artha) is recognized, there the understanding of the lily and so forth occurs through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Where, however, there is no understanding in the form of "lily-ness" (kumuda-tva)...

They say that there is knowledge of the intended meaning (tātparya) and a sublation of the literal sense of "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*); in that case, the comprehension is accomplished through the power of the word's components alone. Indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is a relation with the primary meaning (*śakya*), arising from the impossibility of the intended meaning. It is held that proximity (*āsatti*), compatibility (*yogyatā*), expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and knowledge of the intended meaning (*tātparya-jñāna*) are required [for verbal comprehension].

82. Where, as in the case of *sthalapadma* ("land-lotus") and the like, the meaning of the individual components (*avayavārtha*) is sublated, there the cognition occurs in the form of "lotus-ness" (*padmatva*) by virtue of the power of the whole (*samudāyaśakti*). However, if the land-lotus is indeed of a different genus (*vijātīya*), then it occurs only through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). But where the etymological meaning (*yaugikārtha*) and the conventional meaning (*rūḍhyartha*) exist independently [of one another]...
Bodha (cognition) is that which is both etymological and conventional, such as the word *udbhid* and others.

For in that case, the term *udbhid* brings to mind both a tree, shrub, or the like—which is the agent of breaking forth—and also a specific sacrifice. 81. Regarding the definition "lakṣaṇā is a relation with the denoted meaning":
in examples such as "a hamlet on the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*), [it refers to] the denoted meaning of the word *gaṅgā*.

Where the impossibility of the connection of the primary meaning (ghoṣa) with the form of a "flow" (*pravāha*), or the impossibility of its intended purpose (*tātparya*), is recognized, there the understanding of the "bank" (*tīra*) occurs through indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And that [indication] consists in a relationship with the primary meaning (*śakya*). For instance, because a relationship between the primary meaning in the form of a flow and the bank has been apprehended.

There is the recollection of the bank; from that, the verbal comprehension [of the sentence] arises. However, if the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) were the sole basis for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), then in such cases as "Bring in the staffs" (*yaṣṭīḥ praveśaya*), there would be no figurative indication, because there is no impossibility of the syntactic connection of the act of entering with the staffs themselves. Therefore—
In the case of "entering that," because the intended meaning (tātparya) of eating is untenable, there is a secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) of the term "staff-bearers.

Similarly, in expressions such as "Let the curd be protected from crows," the word "crow" has a secondary signification of "anything that spoils the curd," since the intended object of the purpose is the protection of the curd from all [spoilers]. Likewise in cases such as "The umbrella-bearers are going."

When the word *cchatrin* (umbrella-bearer) signifies traveling in a single caravan, there is metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). This very [process] is called "metaphorical indication that does not abandon its own primary meaning" (*ajahatsvārthā lakṣaṇā*), because the two meanings denoted by the word *cchatrin* are understood through the form of traveling in a single caravan. If, however, the impossibility of syntactic connection (*anvayānupapatti*) were the sole basis for metaphorical indication, then in some cases the word *gaṅgā*...
