In that case, there would be no rule that the indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *doṣapada* occurs only in certain instances, such as fish and so forth, on the bank. However, this must be understood: if the relation with the primary meaning is apprehended in the form of "bank-ness," then there is a cognition of the bank as "bank-ness. But if it is [apprehended] in the form of "the bank of the Gaṅgā," [then the cognition is different].

At that time, remembrance occurs by means of that very form [the secondary meaning]. For this reason, there is no secondary signification (lakṣaṇā) with respect to the delimitor of the indicated object (lakṣyatāvacchedaka); for a cognition having that as its qualifier is possible therein even without secondary signification. However, by this same logic, there would be no primary denotative power (śakti) even with respect to the delimitor of the denoted object (śakyatāvacchedaka).

It should be understood that it is easy to state that the capacity of a word consists in its ability to produce a recollection of its denoted meaning (śakyārtha) characterized by that [specific] mode. However, where there is an indication (lakṣaṇā) consisting of a mediated relationship with the denoted meaning, that is called "indication of the indicated" (lakṣitalakṣaṇā). For example:

In a word such as *dvirepha*, the connection with two *repha*s (the letter *r*) is known in the word *bhramara*, and the connection of the word *bhramara* is known in the bee; this is *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*. However, a word possessing secondary meaning (*lākṣaṇika*) is not itself the cause of comprehension. Rather, it is another word that serves as the cause for the verbal cognition of the secondary meaning.

This is because words are determined to possess the capacity to produce a verbal cognition of their own denotable meaning as related to the meanings of other words through either a primary (śakti) or secondary (lakṣaṇā) relation. Since there is no primary power (śakti) in a sentence, there can likewise be no secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), which consists of a relation to that which is denotable. This is the case in such instances as "A hamlet on the deep river... (*gabhīrāyāṃ nadyāṃ ghoṣaḥ*).

Thus it has been stated that, in that case, there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word "river" as meaning "the riverbank," and the referent of the word "deep" is construed with the river through non-difference (*abheda*), since in some instances even partial construal (*ekadeśānvaya*) is accepted.
If, however, partial construal is not accepted there, then [the word] "river"—

In the phrase "on the bank of the deep river" (*gabhīranadītīre*), the word *lakṣaṇā* indicates that the term *gabhīra* (deep) functions as a determiner of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). The same applies in the case of a *bahuvrīhi* compound. For in such cases—as in the word *citragu* ("one who has brindled cows")—if one accepts partial co-referentiality (*ekadeśānvaya*), then there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *go* (cow) in the sense of the owner of the cow, and the word *citrā* (brindled) is construed in non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with the cow [as the object of the signification]. If...

If partial inherence (ekadeśānvaya) is not accepted, then in the case of "the owner of a brindled cow" (*citragu*), there is a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word *go* (cow) as referring to the owner of the brindled cow, while the word *citra* (brindled) serves to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Similarly, in the case of "the tree climbed by a monkey" (*ārūḍhavānaro vṛkṣaḥ*), there is a secondary indication of the word *vānara* (monkey) as referring to the act of climbing performed by the monkey, while the word *ārūḍha* (climbed) serves to indicate the intended meaning.

The same applies elsewhere as well. However, in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the first member. For instance, in a word such as *rājapuruṣa* ("king's man"), the meaning of the word "man" does not directly connect with the meaning of the word "king," because it is an unestablished rule of grammar that two nominal meanings—other than those involving particles (*nipāta*)—can be related to one another through a relation of difference (*bheda*).

Otherwise, even in the case of "the king is a man," there would be such a comprehension of the relation [between the two nouns]. In "the cloth is not a jar" and similar instances, because the negative particle (*nañ*) is directly construed with both "jar" and "cloth," the phrase "other than a particle" (*nipātātirikta*) is included [in the definition]. This is also the case in "the blue jar" and so forth.

It cannot be argued that the memory of the elided case-ending must be postulated [as the cause of understanding], because comprehension arises even from that [word] for one who has not remembered the case-ending. Therefore, in the word *rājapuruṣa* and similar compounds, there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of "one related to the king," and this [relation] is construed as non-difference (*abheda*) with the man. But in a copulative compound (*dvandva*), as in *dhavakhadirau*...

In expressions such as "cut [the two]," the *dhava* and *khadira* trees are understood through the dual number of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) as being qualified by duality; in this case, there is no secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*). Nor should it be argued that there is secondary signification in the sense of "conjunction" (*sāhitya*), because we observe the use of the copulative compound (*dvandva*) even for things devoid of conjunction. Furthermore, it should not be argued that conjunction consists in the state of being connected to a single action.

Because we observe expressions such as "Look at the *dhava* and *khadira* trees" or "Cut [the *dhava* and *khadira*]," and because their coexistence (*sāhitya*) is not experienced [as a distinct entity], therefore coexistence and the like are not the meaning [of the compound]. For this very reason, in the case of the injunction "The king and the priest, desiring union, should sacrifice," a copulative compound (*dvandva*) is adopted due to the absence of any need for figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). However—

A copulative compound (*dvandva*) occurs where there is a real distinction [between the members]. It should not be asked how this applies in cases such as "there is no non-difference between the blue and the jar," for in that instance, the word "blue" has a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*) in its blueness, and the word "jar" has a secondary meaning in its jar-ness;
and the term "non-difference" means "non-difference of substrata. However, if it were a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*), [the following would apply].

If it is argued that the aggregate (*samāhāra*) is also experienced [as denoted], then in cases such as *ahinakula* ("the snake and the mongoose"), there is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the subsequent member for the aggregate of the snake and the mongoose; the preceding member serves merely to indicate the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*). Furthermore, how can the aggregate be construed in an expression such as *bherīmṛdaṅgaṃ vādaya* ("play the drum and the kettle-drum")?
It should not be argued that such [number] is impossible because it is a specific form of relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*);

for it is connected to that [cognition] through a mediated relation (*paramparāsaṃbandha*). The same applies in cases such as "the five roots" (*pañcamūlī*) and so on. Others, however, maintain that in expressions such as "snake and mongoose" (*ahinakūla*), both the snake and the mongoose are understood, and the number one is construed with each individually.

The technical designation *samāhāra* (aggregation) applies only where unity and neuter gender are prescribed by the rule beginning with *prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām*. Elsewhere, they state that the singular number is incorrect. In cases such as *pitarau* ("parents") and *śvaśurau* ("parents-in-law"), the word *pitṛ* refers to both the progenitor and the mother, and the word *śvaśura* [refers to both the father-in-law and the mother-in-law].

There is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in cases such as "the husband and wife" [referring to a specific couple] or "womenfolk. The same applies elsewhere. However, there is no indication in cases such as "pots," because it is possible for various individual pots to be presented through the form of potness (*ghaṭatva*). But in the case of a *karmadhāraya* compound, such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), the referent of the word "blue" is related to the referent of the word "lotus" by way of the relation of identity (*abheda*).

And in that case, there is no indication (lakṣaṇā). For this very reason, in the injunction "one should cause a Niṣāda-sthapati to sacrifice," it is not a *tatpuruṣa* compound because that would entail indication; rather, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound because there is an absence of indication. Nor can it be argued that since the Niṣāda—a specific mixed caste—is ineligible for the Vedas, officiating as a priest is impossible for him.

This is what must be said: because the application of learning (vidyā) to the Niṣāda is postulated from that very [textual] source; and because, by virtue of parsimony (lāghava), when the primary meaning is construed, the postulation [of a secondary sense] due to its incompatibility is not a fault, as it constitutes a "weightiness resulting from the fruit" (phalamukha-gaurava).
In cases such as *upakumbham* ("near the jar") and *ardhapippalī* ("half a pippalī"), there is indication (lakṣaṇā) in the subsequent word for that which is related to it.

And the comprehension of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) occurs by virtue of the primacy of the meaning of the prior member. Thus, there is no semantic power (*śakti*) whatsoever in a compound, since its function is accomplished solely through the powers of the individual words. "Proximity" (*āsatti*), and so forth:
[these refer to] the cognition of proximity, the cognition of compatibility (*yogyatā*), the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), and the cognition of intention (*tātparya*).

[This is] the cause for verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Regarding that, he states the nature of *āsatti* (proximity): "But proximity... etc. *Āsatti* is the non-interruption between two words that stand as the relatum (*anuyogin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of the syntactic connection (*anvaya*); the knowledge thereof is the cause for verbal cognition. This is because, even in some cases where there is an interval, verbal cognition occurs due to the illusion of non-interruption.

Some [hold this view]. In reality, however, since knowledge of non-intervention is not required, the cause of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) is the presentation of those two word-meanings in non-intervened succession, when the co-referential connection (*anvaya*) of one word-meaning with another word-meaning is required. Therefore, in cases such as "The mountain, Devadatta, has eaten fire" (*girir bhuktaṃ agnimān devadattena*), [this condition is not met].

There is no verbal cognition [arising from the mere proximity]. In cases such as "The blue pot is a substance; the cloth [is a substance]," verbal cognition arises due to a misconception regarding proximity (*āsatti*). Even if there is no verbal error when there is a misconception regarding proximity, there is no deficiency [in our theory]. Now, consider where it is said: "Devadatta is the one with the umbrella, the one with the earrings, and the one with the garment."

If it is argued that, because the recollection of the preceding word is destroyed by the recollection of the subsequent word, it is impossible to have a recollection of each word without interruption, we say no;
for [the recollection occurs] through the final [recollection] produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) generated by the experience of each individual word.
The recollection of all those words arises without interruption;

for just as a single perception can arise from multiple sense-contacts, so too the arising of a single recollection from multiple latent impressions (saṃskāras) is possible, since the cognition of the final phoneme, accompanied by the latent impressions of all those preceding words, acts as the awakener (udbodhaka).

Otherwise, how could there be the recollection of a single sentence from various phonemes? However, some maintain that once those word-meanings have been recollected, there occurs simultaneously—by way of the analogy of birds in a nest—a verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) consisting of the understanding of the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) among those word-meanings as action and object, according to the maxim of the young and the old. "The elders, the youths..."
"Just as these young pigeons fly down onto the threshing floor simultaneously,

so too do all word-meanings become mutually connected at once. Others, however, hold that "whatever is required, is suitable, and comes into proximity, by each of those [factors] is its own meaning (svārtha) connected."

"It is understood by the words alone. Likewise, they also say that after the comprehension of the meaning of the constituent parts (khaṇḍavākya), the comprehension of the meaning of the great sentence (mahāvākya) occurs through the recollection of the word-meanings in that very same manner. By this, the "word-sphoṭa" (padasphoṭa)—which is manifested by the phonemes (varṇa)—is also refuted.

[The meaning is grasped] through the perception of the final phoneme accompanied by the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes, by that very [cognition] which manifests it. However, this must be understood:
where "the door" is said, the comprehension occurs from the knowledge of the word "close" (*pidhehi*) alone, and not otherwise.

Because the knowledge of meanings such as "covering" [is required], and because the presentation (*upasthiti*) of each respective word-meaning generated by each word is the cause for the corresponding verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Furthermore, since verbs and objects are expected (*ākāṅkṣita*) only in their respective forms, how could [a cognition] arise without a verb?

[Otherwise] there would be a lack of understanding. Likewise, in cases such as "puṣpebhyaḥ" (from flowers), since the dative case is otherwise untenable without the ellipsis of a word such as "spṛhayati" (he desires), the ellipsis of a word is necessary. He defines semantic competency (*yogyatā*)—as in "padārtha"—[stating that] it is the cause.

"Proximity (sannidhāna), however, is said to be the non-separation of words. In that context, fitness (yogyatā) regarding the word-meaning is proclaimed to be [the capacity] of that which possesses it [to relate]. (83) The meaning is that fitness is the relation of one word-meaning with another word-meaning.
And because of the absence of knowledge of that, there is no [cognition of sentence-meaning] in cases such as 'he sprinkles with fire'."

Verbal cognition. Now, an objection: it might be argued that the knowledge of this compatibility (*yogyatā*) is not possible everywhere prior to verbal cognition, because the meaning of the sentence is something previously unknown (*apūrva*). This is not so; for when there is recollection of the respective word-meanings, [the knowledge of compatibility arises] in some cases as a form of doubt and in other cases as a form of certainty.

[The Naiyāyikas argue: Because the knowledge of compatibility (*yogyatā*) is possible. However, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that the knowledge of compatibility is not a cause of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*). For in cases such as "He sprinkles with fire" (*vahninā siñcati*), there is no [verbal comprehension] because it is obstructed by the ascertainment of incompatibility (*ayogyatāniścaya*), which consists in the absence of fire being the instrument for the act of sprinkling.

Verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*). Regarding the certainty of its absence, it is sufficient for that [cognition] to appear—provided it is not produced by ordinary sense-contact and is not produced by any specific defect—without the use of the word *yat*.
That which lacks the capacity to produce the experience of another [word] is *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy); however, the intention of the speaker is [the cause of verbal cognition].

The intended meaning (tātparya) has been fully explained. [Verse 84] Since the mere cognition of that [object] not produced by a specific defect acts as an obstacle, its status as an obstacle to verbal comprehension (śābdabodha) is established.
Furthermore, they say that the delay in verbal comprehension is not proven to be caused by a delay in the cognition of semantic competency (yogyatā).

82 || 83 || He explains *ākāṅkṣā* (expectancy) with the words "by which word," and so forth. The meaning is: that word together with which another word lacks the capacity to produce a cognition of syntactic connection (*anvaya*) is the expectancy of that [latter] word with respect to that [former] word. Without a verb-word, a case-role word (*kāraka-pada*) does not produce a cognition of connection.

Therefore, it produces an expectancy for that [object]. In reality, however, the mere proximity of words denoting the action and its factors is fulfilled by the condition of *āsatti* (contiguity). Nevertheless, with respect to the cognition of the objecthood (*karmatā*) of a jar, the knowledge of the expectancy in the form of the accusative case-suffix following the word "jar" is the cause. Thus, "the jar..."

In cases such as "karmatvam ānayanam kṛtiḥ" (the objecthood is the bringing, which is the effort), there is no verbal comprehension [of the relation between the terms]. However, in cases such as "athāyam eti putro rājñaḥ puruṣo 'pasāryatām" (now this son of the king comes; let the man be removed), because there is an apprehension of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) regarding the word "king" together with the word "son," the verbal comprehension occurs through that very [intention]. This is so provided that the apprehension of the intention is with respect to the "man."

However, the inferential understanding (anvaya-bodha) along with that [intention] would certainly occur. He explains *tātparya* (speaker's intention) as "the desire of the speaker. If the knowledge of *tātparya* were not the cause, then in cases such as "bring the *saindhava*," there would be no distinction between the understanding of a horse in some instances and salt in others.

It might be argued: "Let context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors that apprehend the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) be causes for verbal cognition. But this should not be said, because they lack a commonality (*ananugama*).
If one were to establish their commonality by way of their being generators of the knowledge of intention, then the knowledge of intention itself [is the cause], due to parsimony (*lāghava*).

Let there be a cause. And thus, even in the case of the Veda, God is postulated for the sake of knowing the intended meaning (*tātparya*). Nor should it be argued that in that case, the knowledge of the teacher’s intention is the cause; for at the beginning of creation, there is no teacher. Nor can it be said that there is no dissolution at all, such that where would the beginning of creation occur?
It must be stated [that this is so] because dissolution (*pralaya*) is taught in the Āgamas.

And thus, even in the case of the words of a parrot, the knowledge of the intention belonging to God (*īśvara*) is the cause. However, in the case of the contradictory words of a parrot, it must be stated that the knowledge of the intention of the trainer alone is the cause. Others, however, [hold this view] regarding polysemous words and the like.

In some cases, the knowledge of the speaker's intention (*tātparya*) is the cause [of verbal cognition]; thus, in the case of the words of Śuka, there is verbal comprehension even without the knowledge of intention. However, regarding the Veda, they say that the determination of the meaning is achieved through principles refined by the beginningless study of Mīmāṃsā. (84)
Thus ends the section on Verbal Cognition (*śabdakhaṇḍa*) in the *Siddhāntamuktāvalī*, composed by the venerable Vaśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. 4.
The Investigation of Recollection (Smaraṇanirūpaṇam) 5: Previously, it was stated that cognition is of two kinds based on the distinction between experience (*anubhava*) and recollection (*smaraṇa*).
Among those, the types of experience have been shown; however, recollection has not been shown because it is easy to understand. Regarding that:

For indeed, prior experience is the cause. On this point, some maintain that it is not the state of being an experience (*anubhavatva*) that constitutes causality, but rather the state of being a cognition (*jñānatva*) alone; otherwise, there would be no recollection following a recollection, because the prior latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would have been destroyed by the recollection of the same type. In my view, however...

They say that by that very first recollection, through the medium of another mental impression (*saṃskāra*), a subsequent recollection is produced. Based on the context of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika epistemology, the argument would typically continue by stating that the result (the final recollection) does not arise because the required auxiliary cause—the residual impression (*saṃskāra*) from the collective cognition—is either destroyed or insufficient to produce a simultaneous recollection of all items. Since time or disease lacks the capacity to destroy mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), it must be stated that the final fruit [of karma] is what destroys the impression; and thus, there is no impossibility of successive recollections. This is because the firm presence of the immediate activator constitutes the meaning of the term "proximity" (sannikarṣa).
Nor should it be argued that, due to a lack of a deciding factor (vinigamanāviraha), causality would also belong to "cognition-ness" (jñānatva);
for when there is no knowledge of deviation with respect to a specific property, a general property is established as being otherwise accounted for (anyathāsiddha).
Otherwise, how could a staff-bearer not be a cause for the cognition [of a person] as a substance by way of error?
Nor should it be argued that there is a doubt of deviation due to a doubt regarding whether intermediate memories destroy the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*);
for, rather than postulating an infinite number of latent impressions and their destroyers, it is simpler to hold that the final memory alone [destroys them].
Because there is no doubt of deviation [in the inference] by virtue of postulating that [the contact] is the destroyer of the mental impression (saṃskāra).

The Examination of the Mind (6):
The mind is said to be the instrument for the direct perception of pleasure and other sensations; its atomicity is asserted here on account of the non-simultaneity of cognitions.

85. Now, in order to define the mind (*manas*) as it follows in the sequence, he says: "Direct perception" (*sākṣātkāra*). By this, the proof for the existence of the mind is demonstrated. To explain: the direct perception of pleasure has an instrument (*sakaraṇaka*), because it is a produced direct perception (*janyasākṣātkāratvāt*).

The instrumentality of the mind is established by the inference: "like the visual direct perception. Nor should it be argued that, on these grounds, there would likewise have to be other instruments for the direct perceptions of pain and so forth; for, by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), a single [instrument] is established as the instrument for all direct perceptions.

In this way, the existence of the mind (manas) is to be understood through its being the substratum of the conjunction that serves as the non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) of pleasure and the like. Regarding that, he states the proof for the atomicity (aṇutva) of the mind: "Because of the non-simultaneity [of cognitions].
Of cognitions...
It is established by experience that visual, gustatory, and other perceptions do not arise simultaneously— that is, they do not originate at one and the same time.

In this regard, even when objects are present before them, it is due to the connection of certain sense organs with their respective objects that cognition is produced by one organ, while due to the lack of such connection, no cognition is produced by the others.
It is not produced; furthermore, since non-proximity is impossible given the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the mind, the mind is not all-pervasive.
Nor should it be argued that the delay in that cognition at that time is due solely to the delay in the awakening of a specific *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force); for if that were the case...

Otherwise, it would follow that there is no conceptualization even regarding the eyes and other sense organs. Nor should it be asked: "How can there be simultaneous knowledge produced by multiple sense organs in cases such as eating a long roll of food or for those possessing various attentions?
For due to the extreme lightness of the mind, multiple cognitions arise through its immediate connection with multiple sense organs.

This is because the cognition of simultaneity—such as in the case of piercing a hundred lotus petals—is erroneous. Nor should it be argued that both [simultaneity and non-simultaneity] are possible due to the mind possessing contraction and expansion; for that would involve the conceptual burden (*gaurava*) of postulating multiple parts, their destruction, and so forth. By contrast, it is simpler (*lāghava*) to maintain that the mind is partless and atomic in nature.
The summary is that [the distinction] arises from the mental construction (*kalpanā*). Thus, the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*) has been explained. || 85 ||
The Definition of Qualities (Guṇanirūpaṇam) 7. Now, qualities should be known as residing in substances, being themselves devoid of qualities and devoid of action. Having defined substance...
He defines the qualities (*guṇa*) with the words beginning "Now," and so forth. If it is asked what the proof is for the universal *guṇatva* (quality-ness), [the answer is]:

the causality that exists in that which is distinct from substance (*dravya*) and action (*karman*), yet possesses a universal (*sāmānyavat*), must be delimited by some property (*dharmāvachchhinna*), because an unconditioned causality (*niravachchhinnakāraṇatā*) is impossible. For indeed...

Whether [the universal] such as *rūpatva* (color-ness) and so forth is co-extensive with existence (*sat*) or not, it cannot serve as a delimiting factor there because it subsists in a smaller or larger domain; therefore, something common to all twenty-four [qualities] must be stated, and that alone is *guṇatva* (quality-ness). Regarding the phrase "inhering in substances" (*dravyāśritāḥ*):
although inherence in a substance is not the defining characteristic [of qualities] because it overextends to action (*karman*) and so forth, nevertheless...
The meaning of that [term] is: possessing a genus (jāti) distinct from existence (sattā) that delimits the pervasion of substanceness (dravyatva).

For indeed, qualityness (guṇatva) is that which delimits the pervasion of substanceness, and qualities possess it. Neither substanceness nor actionness (karmatva) delimits the pervasion of substanceness, because [the latter] does not exist in space (gagana) and so forth.
Because of the absence of both substance and action, the state of being a substance (*dravyatvatva*) or the state of being a generality (*sāmānyatva*), and so forth, are not *jāti*;

thus, they are excluded. Regarding the phrase "devoid of qualities" (*nirguṇa*): although the state of being devoid of qualities exists in actions and the like as well, it should nevertheless be understood here as "the state of being devoid of qualities while possessing generality and being other than action."

Since universals (jāti) and so forth do not possess the property of being universal, action does not differ from action, and substance is not devoid of qualities, there is no over-extension [of the definition] to those cases. The phrase "devoid of activity" is a statement of their essential nature (svarūpa-kathana), not a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa). [The qualities are: color, taste, touch, smell, priority, posteriority, fluidity... [86] ...[and] viscidity.

The impulses of moisture (snehavega) are considered to be corporeal qualities; these include merit (dharma), demerit (adharma), mental impressions (bhāvanā), sound, and also intellect (buddhi) and the rest.
All these are proclaimed by the learned to be incorporeal qualities. Number (saṃkhyā) and the others, ending with disjunction (vibhāga), are qualities common to both.
[These] are considered [to be nine], because [the definition] would otherwise over-apply to space and so forth. Regarding "form" (rūpa) and "velocities" (vega):
by "velocity," the elasticity of rest (sthitisthāpaka) is also to be implied. Regarding "qualities of the corporeal" (mūrtaguṇāḥ):
the meaning is that they do not reside in incorporeal things. As for the definition:
Thus, the principle of mutual difference applies here as it does in the subsequent cases. Regarding the "immaterial qualities":
conjunctions, disjunctions, numbers such as duality and so forth, and likewise dual separateness and the like—these are qualities that reside in multiple substrata.
Therefore, all remaining qualities are considered [to be otherwise].

Each exists individually. The six beginning with cognition (buddhi) and ending with touch (sparśa), along with natural fluidity (sneha), unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa), mental impression (bhāvanā), and sound (śabda)—these are the specific qualities (vaiśeṣika-guṇas).
Number (saṃkhyā) and so forth, up to non-extremeness (aparatva), as well as non-natural fluidity (asāṃsiddhika-drava), exist in corporeal substances (mūrta). 90–91. Not in [the others].

The meaning is that they "exist. Regarding the phrase "of both": the meaning is the qualities of the formed (mūrta) and the formless (amūrta). || 86 || 87 || 88 || Regarding the phrase "residing in many":
conjunction, disjunction, duality, and so forth, reside in pairs; while triadness, tetradness, and so on, reside in threes, fours, and so forth.
The object of cognition [is as follows]. || 89 || "From this" means:

color, taste, smell, touch, unity, dimension, individuality, priority, posteriority, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, gravity, fluidity, viscidity, mental impression (*saṃskāra*), unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and sound; such is the meaning.
"Buddhyādi" means cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort. "Up to touch" (sparśāntāḥ) means color, taste, smell, and touch. "Fluidity" (dravaḥ) means the state of being liquid.
These—gravity and velocity—are specific qualities (*vaiśeṣika*), while the others are general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*).
[The qualities] beginning with number and ending with remoteness (aparatva), as well as fluidity (dravatva) and viscidity (sneha), have been proclaimed [as perceptible by two senses].

These, however, are perceptible by two senses; those ending with touch (sparśa), along with sound (śabda), are perceptible by one external sense organ (bāhyakaikendriyagrāhya); while heaviness (gurutva), the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), and mental impression (bhāvanā) are [perceptible only by the internal sense]. The suffix *ṭhak* is used in the sense of its own meaning (*svārthe*) to form the word *vaiśeṣika*.
The meaning is "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Regarding "number" (*saṃkhyā*):

the meaning is number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, and posteriority. Those specific qualities of the all-pervading substances which are beyond the senses are produced without [corresponding] qualities in their causes.

...are thus fully described. (94) "By two sense-faculties" means because they are capable of being apprehended by both the eye and the skin. "External" means that color-form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects] are to be grasped by the eye and the other [faculties].
"Of the all-pervading" means...

The meaning is: intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, mental impression, and sound. However, those qualities beginning with touch and ending with [the absence of] color, as well as fluidity of that same kind, are not produced from the qualities of their causes; likewise, viscidity, speed, gravity, singularity, separateness, and dimension [are not so produced] in the effect. || 95 || In the effect—
Those qualities that are produced are preceded by the qualities of their causes, as will be explained in the case of color and so forth;

however, cognition and the rest are not like that, because there is no cause for the self and so on. (90) Elasticity, these [others], conjunction, and disjunction arise from the qualities of their causes.

And these [qualities], as well as velocity (*vega*), are born of action (*karmaja*). In the case of touch, dimension, singularity, separateness, viscidity, and sound, there exists non-inherent causality (*asamavāyitva*) with respect to the specific quality (*vaiśeṣika-guṇa*). 96–97. 91–93.

94. "But those not produced by baking" (*apākajāstu*): It is stated that they are "not produced by baking" because qualities such as color (*rūpa*) produced by baking lack the property of being preceded by the qualities of their causes (*kāraṇaguṇapūrvakatva*). Such [qualities] are "not produced by baking. This should also be understood to apply to unity (*ekatva*). And "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*): although its being produced by action (*karmajanyatva*) is not...

[If it were defined as] similarity [to the effect], it would be over-extensive (ativyāpti) in the case of jars and the like; and it would be under-extensive (avyāpti) in the case of a conjunction produced by another conjunction. Furthermore, the self (ātman) would be a cause only for hot touch and gravity; likewise, it would be so for velocity, fluidity, and the two types of conjunction and the rest. Thus, causality would be of only nine kinds, or else it would be merely local (prādeśika).

It would be a Vaiśeṣika quality, an all-pervading quality, and likewise both conjunction and so forth [would be]. (99) Because [the definition] does not extend to conjunction, it should nevertheless be understood as "possessing a genus that is pervaded by the quality-ness residing in what is produced by action.
The same should be inferred in other cases as well. (95) (96) Regarding the word "pṛthaktva" (separateness), the suffix *tvap*...

One should grasp both unity and separateness for each successive [instance]. By the term "separateness," one-separateness is meant. This would constitute non-inherent causality (*asamavāyikāraṇatva*).
[For example,] the color, taste, smell, and touch of a jar and so forth [arise] from the color, taste, smell, and touch of the potsherds and so forth.

Thus, the status of being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for the dimension and other qualities of a jar and so forth—belonging to the atoms of the potsherds and so on—is established; the same should be understood for sound in relation to a second sound, as well as for elasticity (*sthitisthāpaka*) and singularity (*eka-pṛthaktva*). This refers to their being instrumental causes (*nimittatva*).

The meaning is that [the qualities] such as cognition (buddhi) have desire (icchā) and so forth as their causes. "In two ways" means as non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa) and as efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa). For instance, hot touch is the non-inherent cause of another hot touch, while it is the efficient cause in the production of qualities born of cooking (pākaja). Gravity (gurutva)...

Gravity is the non-inherent cause of falling and the efficient cause of impact. Velocity is the non-inherent cause of velocity and motion, and the efficient cause of impact. Fluidity is the non-inherent cause of fluidity and trickling, and the efficient cause of cohesion.

The conjunction of the drumstick and the drum is the efficient cause (nimitta-kāraṇa) of the sound, while the conjunction of the drum and space is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi-kāraṇa). The disjunction of the two bamboo halves is the efficient cause of the sound, while the disjunction of the bamboo halves and space is the non-inherent cause. It is localized (prādeśika), meaning it does not pervade its substratum (avyāpyavṛtti).
97 || 98 || 99 || Regarding "the visual faculty" (*cakṣurati*): the universal (*jāti*) of "color-ness" (*rūpatva*), however, is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*).

If it is argued that there is no cognition accompanied by the verbal expression "color," let there be no use of the word "color"; nevertheless, a specific universal that persists through blue, yellow, and so forth, is indeed established by experience.

Even when the words "form" (rūpa) or "sound" (śabda) are not employed, there certainly exists a cognition that delineates specific colors, such as "the color blue" or "the color yellow. Form must be graspable by the eye and the perceiver of substances and so forth; likewise, qualities such as blueness and the like are also established by direct perception (pratyakṣa).

Nor should it be argued that because each individual instance of blue color and so forth is unique, "blueness" and the like cannot be a universal (jāti) since they reside in only a single individual; for this is not the case, because blueness and the like possess multiplicity due to being subject to production and destruction—as evidenced by such cognitions as "the blue has perished" and "the red has arisen. Otherwise, [such cognitions would be impossible].

If a single blue [substance] were destroyed, the entire world would become non-blue. Nor should it be argued that this cognition concerns only the production and destruction of the inherence of blue and the inherence of red; for in the cognition, no such inherence is mentioned. Nor can it be said that "this is that very same [thing]."

It should not be argued that identity [of the blue object] follows from the force of perception and from parsimony (*lāghava*), because perception has as its object only that which belongs to the same class—as in the case of [the thought] "this is that very same *gurjarī* [flute]. Furthermore, parsimony is sublated by perception; otherwise, it would follow that even jars and other such things would be identical.

Because it would follow that the cognition of arising and destruction would have inherence (*samavāya*) as its objective support. By this, taste and the other [qualities] are also explained. "Perceptible by the eye" means the state of being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) perceptible by the eye. [This refers to] the auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*) of the eye.
White and so forth may be of many kinds. The same applies hereafter. Regarding the phrase "of substance and so forth":
"perceptual" (upalambhaka) means the cause of perception. He explains this very point with the words "of the eye.
Manifest color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is the cause for the visual perception (*cākṣuṣapratyakṣa*) of substances, qualities, actions, and universals.
"White and so forth are of many kinds.

That color (rūpa) becomes manifold through distinctions such as white, blue, yellow, red, green, brown, variegated (karbura), and so on. Now, how can variegation be a distinct color? It is as follows:
A whole (avayavin) composed of parts such as blue, yellow, and so forth, cannot first be colorless, because that would entail the consequence of its being imperceptible.

Nor does a color such as blue arise as a quality that exists pervasively (vyāpyavṛtti), because it is contradictory for qualities of a pervasive kind to be non-pervasively located even with respect to a delimited portion such as yellow.

Therefore, a heterogeneous variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) is produced in the whole (*avayavin*) by means of constituent parts of diverse kinds. For this very reason, the experience that "this is a single variegated color" occurs, since the postulation of multiple distinct colors would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). And thus, because one must postulate that blue and other colors act as impediments to the production of yellow and other colors [within the same substrate], there is no [such production] in the whole.
The production of yellow and other colors [is explained by this]. By this, touch (*sparśa*) is also explained.

Taste (*rasa*) and the rest are likewise not non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*); rather, there is no fault even in the absence of taste in a composite whole (*avayavin*) produced from constituent parts (*avayava*) possessing various kinds of tastes. In that case, it is the taste of the parts alone that is perceived by the gustatory organ (*rasanā*).

Because the gustatory faculty and the others lack the capacity to grasp a substance, there is no harm even if the whole (*avayavin*) lacks taste. However, the moderns (*navya*) maintain that in that case, multiple colors such as blue and so forth exist only as non-pervasive occurrences (*avyāpyavṛtti*), because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to assume that blue and other colors possess the power to obstruct yellow and other colors. For this very reason, [it is said]: "He who is red by color..."
A bull that is pale on the face and tail, white on the hooves and horns, and dark blue elsewhere is called *nīla*.

Taste (*rasa*), however, is perceivable by the tip of the tongue; it is manifold, beginning with sweet (*madhura*) and so forth. It is eternal in water and other substances where it exists as a fundamental atom (*paramāṇu*), while in other cases it is non-eternal, being produced together with its substrate. || 101 ||
